title: Tracking AI Overviews: What the data actually shows
content:
AI Overviews have shifted how audiences discover brands. Gone are the days when users would click through multiple search results until they found what they’re looking for. Now, AI Overviews answers questions directly on the results page, meaning brands are either cited or ignored without users ever visiting a website.
The changes brought on by AI Overviews mean marketers need to adjust the way they track brand visibility. Here’s what you need to know about tracking AI Overviews and what data actually shows.
Traditional rank-tracking tools cannot measure the exposure generated by AI Overviews, which now sit above featured snippets as the highest-visibility position.
AI Overviews consolidate multiple sources into a single answer, making inclusion — or exclusion — a meaningful driver of both brand perception and traffic. In my experience, this shift catches marketers off guard precisely because their rankings look fine, making the problem invisible until you know where to look.
Volatile citation patterns — Unlike organic rankings, AI Overview citations don’t correlate reliably with ranking position. A page ranking fifth may be cited while the top result is ignored. Tracking reveals which content attributes actually earn inclusion.
Query category variation — AI Overviews appear more often for informational and how-to queries than transactional ones. Knowing which target keywords trigger an overview considerably shapes your content strategy.
Competitive intelligence — If a competitor is consistently cited for your target terms, that’s a strategic signal you can’t act on without visibility.
Measurement gaps — AI Overviews suppress clicks even when rankings hold, creating the “ranking fine, traffic dropping” paradox. Tracking helps explain it.
The way I think about it, tracking AI Overviews is less like checking a dashboard and more like building a case — one data point at a time. It starts with a baseline: a structured snapshot of which queries trigger AI Overviews, which cite your content, and which surface competitors. Without that starting point, there’s no meaningful way to measure change.
From that baseline, each SERP capture adds a data point that either reinforces or challenges what you recorded before. Over weeks and months, those observations become benchmarks — reference points that reflect normal performance and allow you to distinguish meaningful shifts from routine fluctuation.
That distinction is what separates reactive content decisions from informed ones. I’ve put together a five-step checklist below outlining how to put this into practice.
Step 1: Define your keyword set — Identify informational and how-to queries most relevant to your business. Prioritize keywords where you currently rank. Transactional keywords can be deprioritized for this exercise.
Step 2: Establish a baseline — Run your keyword set through your tracking tool and record the initial state: which queries trigger an AI Overview, which cite your domain, and which cite competitors. This snapshot becomes your reference point.
If you’re not sure where to start, HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is a free, one-time diagnostic that shows how your brand currently appears in AI-generated search experiences — a useful starting point before you begin logging data over time.
Step 3: Select your tracking cadence — Weekly is a practical starting point; daily is appropriate for high-priority terms or during active Google update periods.
Step 4: Log citations and mentions separately — Record whether your content receives a citation (a linked source) or a mention (a reference without a link). Keeping the distinction between linked sources and linkless references preserves data integrity over time.
Step 5: Review and act monthly — Aggregate weekly data into a monthly review. Look for patterns: a lack of citations, competitors gaining ground, or content types consistently earning inclusion. Use findings to inform content updates and gap analysis.
I’ve found that expanding AI Overview tracking to new keywords requires a different mindset than traditional rank tracking. A single observation — cited once, or absent once — tells you very little. What matters is the pattern across multiple data points over time.
Filter your keyword set against two criteria: search intent and business relevance. Informational and how-to queries are the highest-priority candidates. From that filtered list, prioritize by volume, competitive importance, and relevance to your content pillars.
AI Overview appearances are not static. A query triggering an overview today may not tomorrow. Treating any single check as a reliable signal produces reactive decisions based on noise.
Understanding how to trigger and interact with AI Overviews manually is the first step in tracking them effectively. The most reliable way to manually trigger AI Overviews is to phrase queries as complex questions. Instead of “best hair conditioner,” try “How do I choose the best conditioner for curly, low porosity hair?” Why and how prompts are more likely to surface an overview than short, vague queries.
AI Overviews don’t draw exclusively from brand-owned content. Google increasingly surfaces user-generated content — Reddit threads, YouTube videos, forum discussions, and third-party reviews — particularly for queries where firsthand experience carries more credibility than brand messaging. UGC platforms are playing an increasingly important role in how AI tools discover and evaluate content.
UGC platforms have established norms around authenticity. Branded or promotional content is routinely flagged or removed, which is counterproductive to earning organic citations. Contribution should follow these guardrails:
The five KPIs below provide a structured measurement framework, followed by an honest account of where attribution breaks down.
Coverage — The percentage of your tracked keyword set that triggers an AI Overview. This establishes the size of the opportunity and should be tracked over time to detect whether Google is expanding or contracting its overview generation in your category.
For teams tracking visibility across supported search engines, HubSpot’s AEO tools provide an ongoing workflow for monitoring brand presence and surfacing optimization recommendations — though coverage is engine-specific and should be applied only where it’s been verified.
Mention Frequency — How often your brand, product, or content is referenced within the AI Overview text, regardless of whether a link is present. Monitor separately from citation data to avoid conflating two distinct forms of visibility.
Citation Coverage — The percentage of tracked keywords for which your domain receives a linked citation. A gap between high mention frequency and low citation coverage may indicate your content is being paraphrased rather than sourced — worth investigating at the page level.
Cited-Page Distribution — Which specific pages are earning citations and how citation volume is distributed across your content. A heavy concentration on one or two pages signals both dependency risk and an opportunity to identify and replicate what those pages do well.
Business-Impact Proxies — Direct revenue attribution from AI Overview citations isn’t currently possible. Useful proxies include organic click-through rate trends on cited pages, changes in branded search volume, and referral traffic from domains that discuss AI Overview appearances.
These don’t confirm causation, but directional movement across multiple proxies in the same period is meaningful context.
HubSpot Smart CRM doesn’t directly attribute traffic to AI Overview citations, but it’s where downstream signals — shifts in branded contact acquisition, lead-source patterns, or pipeline influence — eventually surface. Useful for connecting AI Overview tracking to metrics that leadership recognizes, without overstating what the data can confirm.
Google Search Console does not categorize AI Overview impressions or clicks as a distinct traffic source. There is no mechanism to confirm whether a user clicked through from an AI Overview citation or a standard organic result.
Mention-level visibility generates no trackable referral signal. The metrics above are directional indicators, not closed-loop attribution — decisions made from this data should be treated as informed hypotheses.
Direct traffic attribution from AI Overviews isn’t available through any native analytics platform. GSC doesn’t segment AI Overview clicks from standard organic results, and GA4 doesn’t receive a distinct referral parameter that identifies an AI Overview as the source.
In practice, tracking requires inference and proxy measurement. Isolate pages with consistent AI Overview citations and monitor their organic traffic independently. Click-through rate compression — stable or growing impressions alongside declining clicks — is consistent with AI Overview influence, though not confirmation of it.
Segmenting by query type adds context. Comparing click-through rates between informational queries that trigger overviews and transactional queries that don’t can surface whether AI Overview-prone terms are underperforming relative to their impression volume.
Some teams track branded search volume alongside citation presence, linking AI Overview activity to a business outcome that leadership can readily understand. Demonstrating measurable impact from AI-driven visibility is an increasing priority — and proxy-based frameworks are currently the most honest way to approach it.
Position one doesn’t guarantee citation. A competitor ranking below you may be cited more consistently for your shared target queries. Closing that gap starts with a structured comparison across five dimensions, applied to a reproducible sample of keywords.
Select a fixed sample of 20 to 50 priority informational queries that trigger AI Overviews with reasonable frequency. Run every competitive analysis against this same sample, on the same cadence, using the same tool or capture method. Changing the sample between cycles introduces variables that make comparison unreliable.
Query Coverage — For the queries in your sample, how often does each competitor appear in an AI Overview relative to your domain? Track as a percentage of the sample per domain and update on your standard cadence to detect whether gaps are widening or narrowing.
Mention Share — How frequently each domain is referenced within the AI Overview text across the sample, with or without a link. Compare ratios rather than raw counts to avoid distortion across tracking periods.
Citation Sources — Where each competitor’s cited content lives: blog posts, product pages, documentation, or third-party sources. A competitor earning significant UGC citations signals that the category conversation is happening in spaces where brand content alone can’t dominate.
Cited Content Types — Which formats are earning citations: long-form guides, how-to articles, comparison pages, video transcripts, and data-driven research. Consistent competitor citation through a specific format is a format signal, not purely a quality signal.
Competitor Presence in Your Priority Queries — Queries where your domain is absent but a competitor is cited are your highest-priority content gaps. Examine what cited competitor pages have that yours don’t: length, structure, specificity, data, recency, and directness of answer.
Repeating this analysis monthly against the same sample transforms a one-time audit into an ongoing competitive intelligence practice.
If I had to whittle what earns an AI Overview citation down to one principle, it would be this: answer one question completely rather than many questions partially. Beyond that, certain attributes consistently correlate with inclusion.
Structure — Content that directly and completely resolves a specific query outperforms broad topic coverage. Step-by-step and numbered formats perform well on how-to queries. Clear headers and logical hierarchy make it easier for Google to extract and attribute specific passages.
Depth and specificity — Narrow and thorough outperform broad and shallow. Original data, proprietary research, and precise statistics earn citations because they offer something generic sources can’t replicate. Accurate definitions and technical explanations earn citations on informational queries where Google needs a reliable reference point.
Authority and experience — Content reflecting practitioner knowledge aligns with Google’s stated quality criteria. Established topical authority on your domain correlates with more consistent citation than equivalent content on domains without that track record.
Recency — Matters more for fast-moving categories. Content covering AI, marketing technology, or regulatory topics that no longer reflect current conditions tends to lose citation presence and requires active maintenance.
Content that consistently fails to earn citations includes thin pages that restate common knowledge, conversion-oriented pages where informational value is secondary, and content that requires surrounding context to be useful as a standalone answer.
HubSpot’s Marketing Hub SEO tools can help at this stage — surfacing page-level recommendations around structure, internal linking, and on-page completeness that support citation candidacy without directly measuring AI Overview performance.
Daily tracking is feasible only when structured to surface meaningful signals. Natural AI Overview variability means undisciplined daily monitoring produces more anxiety than insight.
Establish thresholds that define when a change warrants investigation:
Calibrate thresholds to your category’s baseline volatility — wider for high-fluctuation categories, tighter for stable ones.
Assign explicit responsibility for three functions: data capture and logging, threshold alert review, and monthly synthesis and reporting. On smaller teams, these can be one person, but they should be explicitly assigned. Without clear ownership, tracking data accumulates and goes unacted upon.
This cycle doesn’t guarantee citation. It builds a practice of informed experimentation that improves content quality and AI Overview visibility over time.
The hardest part of this process, in my experience, is resisting the urge to treat a tracking finding as a conclusion rather than a starting point for a hypothesis. Translation from observation to action means forming specific hypotheses about why content is or isn’t earning citations, then testing them through targeted changes. No change guarantees inclusion.
Content improvements increase citation candidacy — they don’t guarantee inclusion. AI Overview composition can change with algorithm updates, independent of anything your content does. Frame recommendations to stakeholders as improving quality and candidacy, not as a mechanism for securing placement.
There is no submission process or direct pathway for inclusion. Google determines citation sources through its own evaluation of quality, relevance, and authority.
What’s within your control when optimizing content for AI Overview is making content a stronger candidate. Answer the target query directly and completely. Use clear structure — headers, numbered steps, explicit definitions — that makes passages easy to extract. Build topical authority through depth and consistency over time. Keep content current where recency matters. Ensure pages are technically sound and fully crawlable.
External signals matter too. Content that earns links, mentions, and discussion carries stronger authority signals into Google’s evaluation — a longer-horizon factor, but meaningful for domains building citation presence from a low baseline.
Treat these as investments in content quality that serve multiple purposes — organic performance, reader experience, and citation candidacy — rather than as a checklist engineered specifically for AI Overviews. The latter leads to optimization theater; the former leads to content that is more useful and more likely to be treated as a reliable source.
No single platform currently provides complete AI Overview tracking coverage. Understanding what each tool category does well — and where it falls short — helps teams build a stack that’s honest about its gaps.
No HubSpot tool can replace a dedicated AI Overview tracking platform for teams that need consistent citation monitoring at scale. HubSpot contributes to the content quality, baseline assessment, and downstream reporting layers — not to the core visibility-tracking layer that purpose-built SERP monitoring tools occupy.
Not directly. GSC reports on clicks, impressions, and positions for traditional organic results, but does not break out AI Overview appearances as a distinct data type.
Some indirect signals — impression spikes on informational queries without corresponding click growth — may hint at AI Overview influence, but GSC alone cannot confirm whether your content was cited. Third-party tools purpose-built for AI Overview tracking are required for that visibility.
Most teams prefer weekly as a solid baseline. Daily checks may be warranted during known Google update periods or after significant content changes. For high-priority keyword sets that drive conversions or brand awareness, more frequent tracking helps catch drops before they compound into measurable traffic loss.
A mention occurs when your brand, product, or content is referenced within the AI Overview text. A citation happens when Google links directly to your page as a source. Citations carry a link and the potential for referral traffic; mentions may influence brand perception without driving any click-through. Tracking both separately gives a more complete picture of how your content is being used.
The core approach involves running a defined set of keywords through a tracking tool or via manual SERP capture on a consistent cadence, recording whether an AI Overview appears, whether your domain is cited, and where in the overview your content is referenced.
Platforms like SE Ranking, BrightEdge, and Semrush have introduced AI Overview tracking features that automate much of this. For teams without those tools, a structured spreadsheet logging captures by date and keyword is a functional starting point, though it doesn’t scale.

title: Claude skills vs. plugins vs. MCP connectors: A simple guide
content:
If you’ve opened Claude’s Customize settings and weren’t sure whether a task called for a Skill, a connector, or a Plugin, you’re not alone.
The names sound similar, and people often use them interchangeably in casual conversation even though they do distinct jobs. This guide walks through what each one actually is, how they relate, and which one fits a given workflow, using a real example along the way instead of a hypothetical one.
TL;DR: Skills teach Claude a procedure, MCP connectors give it authorized access to an outside tool or data source, and Plugins package both together so a team can install everything at once.
The easiest way to keep these three straight is to separate access from procedure from distribution. Each layer answers a different question.
A connector links Claude to an outside service — your files, your calendar, an issue tracker, a CRM — through a live connection called an MCP server, which the service itself runs so Claude can reach it. Once you turn a connector on, Claude can read from that service and take action in it, inside your existing permissions.
A skill is a set of written instructions, sometimes with scripts and reference files attached, that Claude loads when your request matches what the skill covers. A skill teaches the how: your team’s report format, your review checklist, the brand voice you always want applied. A skill can tell Claude how to use a connector’s data, but it can’t reach a live service on its own. That’s what the connector is for.
A plugin bundles skills, MCP connectors, commands, and sub-agents into a single package that installs once and can be shared with a whole team, instead of asking every person to add each piece separately.
If you want a broader primer on how plugins work as a category of software, What are plugins? covers the concept outside of Claude specifically. Inside Claude’s ecosystem, a plugin can hold any mix of the pieces above, and installing it adds everything in one step.
A short glossary, since these terms get thrown around loosely:
Picture a request moving through Claude in three stages: a skill can shape how Claude approaches the task, a connector lets Claude reach outside the conversation to get or change real data, and a plugin is the optional wrapper that ships a skill and a connector together as one package.
None of the three sits “above” the others in a power ranking.
A connector without a skill still works fine, as Claude will simply use its own judgment about how to phrase requests to your CRM.
A skill without a connector also works fine — it just can’t touch live data, only whatever you paste into the conversation or whatever else Claude already has access to.
A plugin is only useful when you actually want several of these installed and shared as a unit; a single skill or a single connector doesn’t need one.
Match the problem to the layer, not the other way around:
Combinations are common, and often the right call. A connector supplies the data, a skill decides what to do with it, and a plugin is how both reach everyone else on the team at once.
Take a weekly pipeline review, for example. On its own, none of the three layers gets you the full workflow:
A connector supplies the pipeline context. With the HubSpot Claude connector turned on, Claude can pull deal stages, recent activity, and engagement history straight from HubSpot, scoped to whatever a given user is permitted to see in HubSpot already.
A skill defines the review format. A skill can tell Claude exactly how your team likes a pipeline review structured — which fields matter, how to flag stalled deals, what counts as “needs attention” — so the output looks the same every week regardless of who asks for it.
A plugin packages it for the team. Bundling that skill with the connector into a plugin means a sales manager installs one thing, rather than separately connecting HubSpot and then hunting down the right skill, and rolling it out to a whole team is a single install instead of five.
This pattern is worth building toward because most teams end up connecting to more than one AI tool at once. HubSpot’s own changelog announcing the connector noted that over half of its customers already use multiple LLMs to get work done, which is part of why having your CRM context available consistently, regardless of which layer is doing the work, matters more than picking a single “winning” tool.
Pro tip: Start with the smallest layer that solves the actual problem. If a single skill already gets the format right, don’t reach for a plugin just because it feels more “official.” Package things into a plugin once you’ve confirmed the skill and connector actually work well together and more than one person needs them.
Setup and governance are worth covering together, since the controls at each stage carry over into the next.
Start with one repeatable task rather than trying to stand up your whole stack at once. Pick a process you already do by hand every week, build or find the skill for it, connect the data source it needs, and see whether the combination actually saves time before you package anything for a wider team.
Anthropic’s own skill-creator skill runs a skill against test prompts you define and reports back so you can revise the description or instructions before rolling it out.
When you add an MCP connector, you review and approve the access it’s requesting, and you can set tool-level permissions afterward: Always Allow, Needs Approval, or Blocked, for individual actions rather than the connector as a whole.
Anthropic runs automated validation and a security scan on every plugin version submitted to its public directory, plus a human review before a new listing goes live. That review doesn’t extend to a plugin someone uploads from an unofficial marketplace URL or a local file, so only add those from sources you actually trust.
On Team and Enterprise plans, you can share a plugin with a handful of specific people first, confirm it works the way you expect, and only then set it to install by default or make it required for everyone.
The HubSpot Claude connector , for instance, respects whatever permissions already exist in HubSpot. A rep only sees the pipeline data they’re already allowed to see in HubSpot itself, so existing HubSpot permissions constrain the context available through the connector rather than the connector introducing a separate permission system.
Organization admins on Team and Enterprise plans can see a plugin’s full version history and revert to an earlier version if a new one causes problems, without losing any of the version history in the process.
On Enterprise plans, Organization Owners can export audit log data from Organization settings and Data and Privacy, and the same data is available programmatically through Anthropic’s Compliance API for teams that need to feed it into their own compliance tooling.
None of this amounts to a security or legal guarantee. It’s a description of the controls that exist today, and you should evaluate them against your own team’s requirements rather than treating any of it as a compliance sign-off.
No, not to use ones that already exist. Adding a connector from Anthropic’s directory or installing a plugin is a point-and-click process from Claude’s Customize settings. Writing your own skill from scratch is also mostly writing plain instructions in a text file — no code required unless you want to add an optional script. Building your own MCP connector or submitting a plugin to the public directory is the part that takes engineering work.
A Skill teaches Claude how to do a task; MCP is the protocol that lets Claude reach outside tools and data to get the information it needs to do that task in the first place.
Once more than one person needs the same skill, or the same skill needs to travel together with a specific connector, package it as a plugin. A single skill is fine as long as you’re the only one using it and it doesn’t depend on a connector someone else still has to set up separately.
A “tool,” in Claude’s terms, is usually something a connector exposes — a specific action Claude can take in an outside service. A slash command is a named shortcut, often bundled inside a plugin, that runs a specific skill or action when you type it directly rather than describing the task in plain language. A skill is the instructions themselves; commands and tools are two different ways of triggering something.
Yes. The HubSpot connector for Claude is a working example you can install today. It requires an active HubSpot account on any tier and a paid Anthropic plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise), and it can create and update records like contacts, companies, deals, and tickets, though it doesn’t delete anything on any object.
Skills, plugins, and MCP connectors aren’t competing tiers of the same feature. They’re three different jobs, and the workflows that actually stick tend to use more than one at a time. If you want to see the access layer in action with a real CRM rather than a hypothetical one, the HubSpot connector for Claude is a reasonable place to start, and it pairs naturally with whatever skill or plugin your team builds around it.

title: Why SEO Isn’t Enough Anymore – And Why That’s A Good Thing
content:
SEO has been the most profitable channel by some margin for the last 15 years.
We can debate about the rights and (broadly) wrongs of last-click attribution until the cows come home, but SEO has been the money channel. The channel the execs have leapt at.
But now, the days of traffic for old rope are gone. Audience journeys have become more complicated than ever, and some of the shine has been taken off search.
While it was always over-buffed, you’d be a fool to forget Google. According to all of the clickstream data I’ve seen, the majority of user journeys – regardless of whether it’s AI-led – use Google at some stage. Particularly when they’re close to the point of purchase.
Google sees more than 5 trillion searches per year (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson Bennett)
But you cannot build a brand through Search anymore. If you’re an SME, it’s very tough to break into. These aren’t bad things. It’s so lucrative it should be hard. We need better spam policies from Google and we need them to figure out how to combat the slew of slop AI has turned the internet into.
We need brands that have real presence, heft, quality control and an audience before they start to crack the Search code. Google knows they have a quality problem. They’ve been very slow to act, but I hope that’s about to change.
In the July 2026 snapshot, signs of AI authorship can be found in over one-third of pages published after ChatGPT was released.(Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
As always, read, listen, watch – the choice is yours!
The Helpful Content update was, let’s say, interesting. Interesting in the brands that got nuked by it at least. In the way it was handled. In the subsequent handling of the Site Reputation Abuse update .
And you’re talking to someone who had a small content and price comparison site destroyed by the HCU. And I think they were right to do so. Well, broadly.
Because Google cannot have SEOs ruling the web. Not if they want to create a loyalty ecosystem. The HCU was a clear attempt to purge SEO-first sites. Sites with no wider presence – built by people who were extremely competent at SEO – were exposed.
Content created for search engines was decimated. We’re now seeing something closer to Google’s dream. Where you only rank if you have a profile outside of the search ecosystem and over-optimised content isn’t necessarily a good thing. Worth noting that their dream is very ad and AIO heavy. Make of that what you will.
The fact Search Console now shows you how your social content performs in Search is about as clear a sign as we ever get.
Google’s entire algorithm is a proxy for trust. And what do people trust? People. Which historically has been problematic…
HouseFresh was, or rather is, an independent air-quality review site. According to their own guidelines:
“Every product you read about on HouseFresh has been tested in our home… 130+ products reviewed… 0 sponsored product reviews”
First-hand, expert, original: the content Google’s guidelines ask for.
By their own admission, the HCU took away >90% of their traffic from Search . From over 4,000 daily visitors in September in 2023 to just 200 in early 2024. HouseFresh stated that Google’s March 2024 update finished the job, with spammed Reddit threads and old Quora posts outranking its reviews.
Now, obviously I can’t tell you if HouseFresh were doing all of the right things. Nor do I have the inclination to look. But there was a dirty little pattern that emerged and niche sites bore the brunt of it.
Over this period, Retro Dodo lost 85% of its organic traffic , while Reddit surged by 190% almost directly after signing a deal with Google – albeit one for data-licensing . You could absolutely argue that Reddit became Google’s bastion of first-hand experience – but big sites and publishers were far more resilient.
Other big publishers saw record levels of affiliate revenue.
Even if those publishers showed very little first-hand experience or E-E-A-T that Google so keenly espoused. Really that’s where the crux of the argument lies – Google clearly favored big brands.
The internet needed a change. While this was handled with a level of empathy now synonymous with Silicon Valley (or ICE for that matter), something needed to happen.
Worth noting that HouseFresh has made a strong recovery in Search over the last year or two.
Search makes up nearly 64% of their total traffic (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
But they’re extremely reliant on Search and that’s not where you want to be. I am sure this level of search reliance would’ve been part of the original HCU.
There’s an excellent nugget of information here. Since their recovery, HouseFresh have built a near 30,000 YouTube channel. Much needed diversification that has, ironically, coincided with an uptick in Search.
While sitewide demotions were algorithmically applied to niche sites, the Site Reputation Abuse Update was handled in a much more considered manner.
If the HCU was dealt with with an iron fist, the Site Reputation Abuse Update was a velvet glove. Instead of sitewide demotions, Google used manual actions to remove larger sections of publisher sites from its search results – particularly voucher codes and betting.
This, but at a subfolder level (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
I would argue the quality of their results diminished significantly when they did this.
Who doesn’t want betting advice from fans of The Archers? (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
You could say Google had learned from their mistakes and handled this far more gracefully. With an element of precision. You could also say that Google was protecting its financial interests by taking bigger brands who contribute far more significantly to its advertising ecosystem.
I think this is foundational to how you position yourself as an SEO and how you become more valuable in the market. But giving legitimate business advice.
Right now I think these things apply across all disciplines:
Don’t rely on Google to find your audience for you. Piece together the loyalty signals they’re putting in place to better understand what the next few years will value.
To be a player in search, a strong brand has always helped. Now more so than ever, I think. Personal or otherwise. You need robust direct and branded traffic , strong engagement metrics, and third-party factors that corroborate you are who or what you say you are.
Faking it is becoming more and difficult. With longevity, at least. It is much easier to be successful if people in the owned phase of discovery share your content for you. You have to appear in the right places and build a platform.
The final form of E-E-A-T is social proof, corroborated on and off-site.
86% of Google clicks go to a site the searcher didn’t name . That means only 14% are navigational – of the 5 trillion + searches Google processes each year, that’s a sizeable opportunity to reach people.
In last click attribution, SEO always looks like the hero. But that completely excludes the credit other channels in the top and middle of the funnel warranted.
As the journey is now so complicated, you have to measure incremental uplift. That means, if you run a specific campaign, you need to see how conversion and audience activity changes over the coming weeks and months to assess the impact.
I think that’s a) easier and b) makes for a far more creative ecosystem.
48% of 18-24s prefer to watch (32%) or listen (16%) to news online. 42% prefer to read. The opposite is true of the over 55s. If you have a more defined audience, this is easier to manage. If you’re trying to satisfy a broad sweep of the population, you’re going to have to invest in multimodal content to really cut through.
That applies to search too. Video and creator-led content are booming in popularity, particularly in Google Discover . While Discover may appear to be less-publisher friendly, if publishers invested more seriously in video and building individuals, this wouldn’t be a problem.
Younger audiences don’t seek out news sites or publisher apps. Social is their first touchpoint. The creator wields the power.
According to iPullRank’s latest report , 52.3% of searches by 18-24s end without a click, against 42.7% for 55-64s. 55-64 year olds are 7x more likely to click an advert than the 18-24 cohort.
No one spends time on Google. It is an entirely functional transaction. I need a thing, I am going to find the thing. That is not the case with social channels. Or people. people trust people. They don’t trust brands.
The younger you are, the more these statements resonate.
But there’s an opportunity here. Brands and creators have audiences. They both have different types of trust. Part of your job may be figuring out how to tie these two things together. Leveraging the best part of a creator can be incredibly valuable for a brand and vice versa.
Google has more data about how people interact with the internet than any of us can possibly imagine. They also buy more data than anyone.
The rise of video. Social accounts on Discover and in traditional search. The prominence of Reddit. These are by design. Google has been trying to give rise to real people and opinions so the platform continues to satiate a new, hungry audience.
Google knows trust has moved from mastheads to people.
“Discover will make it easier to “find, follow and engage with creators”.
X, Instagram and YouTube Shorts are already in, with “more platforms to come”.”
If you need more proof, just look at how prominent YouTube and X are in the Discover feed . Google’s attempt to create their own social network of sorts is in full swing.
They don’t want to reward sites where the experience is purely transactional. We’ll show you x for a sneak peak at y. That’s why they’ve launched:
Some publisher traffic was always borrowed. If you built an advertising-led ecosystem based on traffic volume, time is running out. Kick off times, channels, bank holidays – straight facts without stories (outside of breaking news) are not a viable solution anymore.
And that’s a good thing for Search. The ecosystem I mean – we need the quality of results to improve. And the advertising and blatant theft of content to reduce, but that’s another matter entirely.
As an SEO. As a marketer. As a creator. Whichever. You should:
To do all of these things, you need to be better at marketing . Understanding people, not AI. LLMs will continue to change because they are, for want of a better word, basic.
If you focus your time becoming better at writing, data analysis, visualization, video production – literally anything – you will be a more valuable SEO and you will understand the business side of things far more effectively.
We’ve got very used to Google doing the heavy lifting for us. That era is declining and whilst it might still be profitable enough for now, you have to a) build better distribution and b) force your way into Google’s result.
There’s no better way of doing that than by outperforming your expected engagement. And you won’t do that without purposeful distribution .
The Golden Hour rule is one of my favorite marketing fundamentals. Not because it guarantees success or can save your mediocre content. But because it forces you to think about distribution early. Beyond the homepage.
Thinking about purposeful distribution takes you out of SEO and into the realm of, you know, actual marketing.
SEO isn’t enough. You need to be a better marketer. Know your audience and where they spend their time. Do cool stuff. Be interesting. Measure incremental uplift, not last click. Build habits, not sessions. And distribute everything you publish.

title: How To Remove Negative Search Results: What 22,620 Links Reveal via @sejournal, @EraseDotCom
content:
This post was sponsored by Erase . The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.
To remove a negative search result, first identify the website behind it. A Google review, a republished court record, and a Reddit thread may all show up in search, but each requires a different approach.
We analyzed 22,620 links clients sent to Erase.com across about 1,650 websites, with removal work starting between January 1 and September 21, 2026. Eligible Google reviews and republished court records were generally easier to remove. Yelp reviews, Reddit threads, and news stories were much harder.
Those differences matter beyond the search results page. Negative content can also appear in AI-generated answers . Our May analysis for SEJ found AI Overviews showing negative reviews in searches that didn’t ask for them.
Use the findings below to choose the right removal route, set realistic expectations, and understand how long successful removals took. Where full removal isn’t possible, we cover alternatives such as de-indexing, requesting a name edit, or pushing the result down in search.
We looked at 22,620 links clients sent to Erase.com between January 1 and September 21, 2026. They came from about 1,650 websites, and the results split sharply by site.
In this analysis, a successful removal could mean taking a page down, de-indexing it, or removing the client’s name or photo. De-indexing keeps a page out of Google’s search results without taking it offline.
Google reviews made up about half of the links in the category breakdown. That breakdown excludes the image-heavy case described in the methodology.
More than 1,000 websites showed up only once in the data. News links alone came from 708 different outlets, each with its own editors and rules.
Google reviews came down more reliably than almost anything else we handled.
Google lists the reviews it will remove in its prohibited and restricted content policy . The list includes fake reviews, impersonation, harassment, off-topic posts, and personal information. When a review clearly fits one of those, Google usually takes it down.
Republished court records, mugshots, and people-search listings were the most reliable categories and the fastest to remove. The median removal in each took less than two weeks.
Reviews on Yelp, Trustpilot, Indeed, BBB, and Glassdoor rarely came down. Reddit threads and news stories were also harder to remove.
For successful outcomes, the median time was 18 days. Of those, 71% were confirmed within 30 days and 91% within 90 days. These figures describe how long successful outcomes took, not the likelihood that a submitted link would be removed.
Full removals were faster than de-indexing, at a median of 14 days versus 21.
Some successful Google review removals took much longer. About one in 10 took more than 90 days, so don’t give up on a report after a month.
Use these findings to set expectations, then follow the removal route that matches each source.
Group your negative links by website, then check each site’s rules and removal options. Start with the sites that move fast, like court-record and people-search sites. If removal or de-indexing isn’t available, plan to push the link down in search instead.
Choose the route that matches each link’s source: Google reviews | Yelp and other reviews | Court records | Mugshots and people-search | Social posts | News, Reddit and government pages .
Before reporting a Google review, check the platform’s policies and the legal limits on removal requests. The FTC’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. It bars businesses from using threats, intimidation, or false accusations to get a review removed.
Google reviews accounted for 82% of our review work. Yelp made up about half of the rest, with more than 1,000 links across its U.S. and Canadian sites. Very few of those Yelp reviews came down.
Compare the review with that site’s rules. In our data, review sites other than Google left reviews up far more often.
If a Yelp or Trustpilot review breaks no rule, a short, factual public reply is usually the better move.
Court record sites such as Trellis , UniCourt , Justia, CaseMine, vLex, and CourtListener usually removed or de-indexed the records we handled. These sites copy filings from court websites. De-indexing means Google stops showing the page, but the page still exists. More than a quarter of successful court-record cases involved de-indexing rather than full removal.
Find Republished Court Records, Then Request Host Removal
The court’s own record rarely changes, so start with the copies. Here is how removal from court record sites works .
Mugshot sites, including Mugshots.zone , Arrests.org , RecentlyBooked, and BustedNewspaper, usually took listings down. We keep a guide for each of these sites .
People-search sites list home addresses and phone numbers. Opt-outs on Whitepages, TruePeopleSearch, Radaris, Spokeo, and FastPeopleSearch usually worked. As our August SEJ article explained, listings can come back when a site refreshes its data.
Instagram posts came down most often, followed by posts on Facebook and X. TikTok and YouTube were the hardest social platforms in our data when there wasn’t a clear copyright or harmful content concern.
Check the post against the platform’s rules on impersonation, harassment, or sharing private information. For photos, check whether the post raises a copyright or privacy issue under that platform’s rules.
If a social post breaks a platform rule, report it under that rule. A post that only criticizes someone or contains commentary covered by fair use is much more difficult to remove. If removal isn’t an option, plan to push it down in search instead.
News stories, Reddit threads, and government pages were the hardest to remove, along with most review sites other than Google.
News links came from 708 outlets, and most outlets left the story up unless there was a material reason for removal or a change in circumstances since publication. When an outlet did act, it often stopped short of deleting the story. About one in four successful news outcomes was a name removal , a photo removal, or de-indexing. It helps to know what news outlets will usually agree to before you ask.
If full removal isn’t possible, ask for less. A news site may agree to take your name out of a story or keep Google from indexing the page. Either change affects what people see when they search your name.
Reddit made up 260 links, and threads rarely came down. Moderators remove posts that break subreddit or site rules; being unflattering alone is not a rule violation. See when a Reddit thread can be removed .
If you prefer to hire a provider rather than handle these requests yourself, ask these four questions.
If you want a second opinion, send us your links. We’ll tell you which ones are likely to come down and how long each should take.
Erase.com analyzed 22,620 of the links sent to us for removal, with work starting between January 1 and September 21, 2026. We counted a link as removed if it was taken down, de-indexed, or had the client’s name or photo taken out. Links the client paused or canceled were excluded from outcome comparisons.
This data doesn’t cover all of our work. It excludes work for clients on subscription and retainer-based removal plans such as data broker removals and our copyright takedowns for sensitive images, which we run as separate programs.
One case with about 3,500 image links is part of the 22,620 total, but we left it out of the category numbers so it wouldn’t skew them. Timing figures cover 13,482 links removed in that period, including some work that started in late 2025. They are measured from the start of work to the confirmed outcome.

In-Post Images: Images by Erase. Used with permission.

title: Your Store Is ‘Agent-Ready’ By Default, We Tested 122 Shopify Stores To See What That Actually Means via @sejournal, @billhunt
content:
In September 2026, Slobodan Manic argued that the text-only versions of websites now being served to AI “strip out the wrong layer.” A markdown mirror describes the page but drops everything a visitor could press, so it becomes “a brochure … served to the user most eager to act.”
He ends with a brilliant three-part list that every ecommerce team should adopt: expose what can be done, make it callable , and report what happened.
I had been running an audit of the top 122 Shopify storefronts with a related question: not whether AI can find or cite these stores, but whether an agent can actually resolve a purchase decision on them. That means having enough information, context, rules, and the capability to execute to answer the buyer’s questions, commit to the purchase, and deal with what comes after.
His article prompted me to go further. Instead of counting which tools the stores declared, I called them. This article reports what we found, confirms his argument, shows where our results differ, and outlines what both merchants and Shopify can do about it.
The platform installed the actions, not the merchants. Manic reports that Shopify switched on WebMCP tools for every Liquid storefront on August 5, and that “the merchants did not build it.” Our data shows the same thing at scale:
If you count adoption of agents.md as a sign of merchant readiness, you are really measuring Shopify’s rollout schedule.
GEO does not address the action. Manic writes that GEO “has absolutely nothing to do with the action.” Our data backs this up. Most stores publish the facts an agent needs, and Shopify’s checkout works. What breaks is the step in between: turning a published policy into an answer the agent can use when making its decision. The return window appears as prose on a policy page, but the agent can’t retrieve it when asked. Being cited or ranked doesn’t fix that.
The semantic floor is broken, including on product pages. He cites WebAIM’s 2026 finding that unlabelled form inputs appear on 51% of home pages, empty links on 46.3%, and empty buttons on 30.6%. We ran the same checks on the product page, where the purchase action actually lives, for the 68 stores we could retrieve:
The buy button itself is usually fine. When it is present, it is a native, named <button> 92% of the time. The problem is around it. If two-thirds of size selectors have no label, an agent cannot reliably tell which dropdown sets the size and which sets the color.
This is where UX, accessibility, and agent readiness must work together because they depend on the same markup. A labeled size selector, a named buy button, and an announced “added to cart” message serve a screen-reader user, a keyboard user, and a browser agent at once. The conflicts stem from a visual-only design: swatches with no names and confirmations that only appear on screen. Fix the markup once and all three benefit.
Huge props to Shopify as nobody else has deployed an agent-callable commerce surface at this scale, and that deserves recognition before any criticism.
Across our sample, 89 of 122 stores answered a standard MCP tool listing. Shopify says its catalog now spans “billions of products across millions of merchants,” and that orders from AI-powered searches grew nearly 13 times year over year in Q1 2026 . Merchants on the platform received catalog search, cart, checkout, and policy lookup tools without writing a line of code.
The quality is also better than I expected. We ran a live, non-completing checkout on every store that exposed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) endpoint: create a checkout for one in-stock item going to a Boston address, read it back, cancel it, then cancel it again. We never completed a purchase or sent payment details.
This bears directly on the third item on Manic’s list. He describes an agent that re-submitted a form because the only confirmation was “rendered for eyes.” On Shopify’s tool layer, that failure is handled: the second cancel is refused with a machine-readable error instead of being silently repeated. On that test, Shopify’s tools already report back to the agent properly.
These are differences of timing and scope, not disagreements.
1. We Tested A Different Door, And Shopify Has Since Finished His
Shopify offers agents two routes into checkout. The first is a server endpoint that an agent calls directly, with no browser (UCP over MCP). The second is WebMCP: tools that register inside the shopper’s own browser tab . Manic tested the browser route on August 6 and found that “the buying path died on an internal error.” At that point, the browser tools covered the storefront and cart, and the checkout step mostly moved the tab to the checkout page.
Our updated September test used the server route. Checkout creation succeeded on every store we gave a real, in-stock item, with a median response time of about 1.1 seconds. The only failures came from our own stale data. We had collected item IDs a few weeks earlier. By test day, five of those items had sold out, and two IDs no longer existed. The stores rejected them with clean out_of_stock or invalid codes (“The merchandise with id … does not exist”). So our result does not show that his defect was fixed. We were testing a different route.
That small failure is still a lesson for merchants, because agents work the same way we did. An assistant may hold an item ID from a product feed, an earlier conversation, or a shared cart, and try to buy it days later. A sold-out item is normal commerce, as long as every surface an agent reads reports availability promptly. A vanished ID is avoidable. It usually happens when a product is deleted and re-created, or re-imported, instead of edited, and the agent then has to start its search over. Keep variant IDs stable, and keep inventory current across your feeds and catalog .
Then, on September 28, Shopify announced support for WebMCP in checkout . Browser agents can now “read and update Shopify checkouts,” covering “the full shopping journey… through checkout and order confirmation,” with no merchant configuration. On September 30, we ran a new test and opened live checkouts at a sample of sites in a browser, with WebMCP exposed to the page. Both registered the four announced tools: get_checkout, update_checkout, complete_checkout, and navigate_to_storefront. A read-only get_checkout call returned the full checkout: line items, totals with tax, fulfillment method, and coded messages showing which fields were still missing. We did not submit an order, but the browser route that failed for Manic now reaches and reads the checkout properly.
The tool descriptions also answer his point about agents repeating actions. They tell the agent to “use get_checkout to verify the outcome” and “do not resubmit while status is complete_in_progress or completed.” That’s the “report what happened” requirement, written directly into the tools.
Every one of the 74 checkouts came back with the status requires_escalation and a message flagged requires_buyer_input. This matches the rule in Shopify’s default agents.md that checkout requires human approval. That is a reasonable safety choice, and it changes what “agent-ready” means. The new browser tools keep the same rule: complete_checkout is to be used “only after the buyer authorizes the purchase,” and control goes back to the buyer for steps such as 3D Secure . On Shopify today, the agent builds a priced cart, and a person commits the money.
An agent can act on a decision only after making one. Manic’s framework covers the doing. Our audit asked whether the agent has what it needs to make a decision and whether it can undo the result. On both, the answer was mostly no, and the September 28 release doesn’t change that. In the browser checkout, the refund terms still reach the agent only as a link to the refund policy page, not as values. get_checkout reads “post-completion order details,” but no tool cancels or changes the order. At one site, the checkout also contained a line item the shopper hadn’t chosen, “Free Returns Coverage” for $2.98, added by the store. The agent can see it, but nothing in the checkout data marks it as optional or explains how to remove it. That’s a rule the buyer needs before committing, and it’s exactly the kind of thing the tools don’t explain.
This is the part I most want ecommerce leaders to take away. It is easy to look at a Shopify store today and conclude it is agent-ready : the agents.md file exists, the UCP profile exists, the MCP tools answer, and many readiness checkers will score the store well.
What the defaults don’t give you: declared is not the same as done.
The agent can’t find the answers to buyers’ questions. Every store with Shopify’s policy tool was asked six questions that a real buyer would ask. We then ran a control test with broad, policy-style questions.
Return windows are the one clear success. For everything else, the content is there, and the tool can reach it when the question sounds like a policy page. It cannot reach it when the question sounds like a buyer. One store’s FAQ says “free standard ground shipping on U.S. orders over $75,” and that answer never comes back for a question about what shipping costs.
Worse, when asked about cancellation, two stores instead returned their shipping FAQ. A wrong answer that looks confident is more dangerous than no answer, because an agent has no reliable way to tell it doesn’t address the question.
Delivery date is missing everywhere. A live checkout priced shipping to Boston for 36 of 74 stores, so for half the sample you can get the cost, but only by starting a purchase. None of the 74 returned an arrival estimate or a carrier, even though the protocol has fields for both. “When will it arrive?” could not be answered through any agent path on any store we tested.
Pickup is invisible. All 93 stores with a UCP fulfillment declaration list shipping as the only method; none declares pickup. That includes retailers that clearly offer it. A store that documents Pickup in Store, yet its agent endpoint answers “No pickup locations available.” Another offers Click & Collect and declares shipping only. Here, the agent gets a clear, machine-readable answer that is wrong, and it will send the customer to delivery when same-day collection was available.
Most policy information isn’t machine-readable . 70% of the stores whose policy text we could read state a return window in prose. Only 7% of product pages expose it as structured merchantReturnDays.
Nothing can be undone. Not one of the 122 stores exposes a tool to cancel, change, or return an order after it is placed. This is not the merchants’ fault. The UCP order specification defines two operations, reading an order and an order-event webhook, and no operation to cancel or amend one ( UCP ). It even defines a permission scope for “cancellation, returns, and other modifications” without defining how to perform any of them.
Across all nine checks we used to decide whether an agent could complete a purchase decision, zero of 122 stores passed. The best were three stores that reached seven of nine. All three failed the same two: no stated cancellation window, and no way to cancel.
When we sorted the failures by the team that owns the missing information, a pattern appeared:
None of these teams owns the website. The checks nearly every store passes are the ones the platform generates automatically: catalog, variants, price, checkout. The ones nearly every store fails to meet need someone outside the web team to write a commercial rule and a system to enforce it. That is an organizational problem, and the search team cannot fix it alone .
Because Shopify is deployed at this scale, it can also fix much of this at scale. Several of the gaps involve data Shopify already holds in structured form.
You do not need a full audit to find out where your store stands. Most of this takes an afternoon.
Ask your own policy tool the questions buyers ask. This one call shows you what an agent gets back:
Repeat it for the return window, shipping cost, arrival time at a real address, pickup today, and used or open-box returns. If you get an empty list, a link, or the wrong topic, that’s what the agent gets too.
Manic’s closing line is that a text-only version of a site is a brochure. Our data adds a second half. Shopify has given its merchants a working checkout that an agent can operate. What it hasn’t yet given them, and what most haven’t provided themselves, is the rulebook an agent needs to use it responsibly: how much, how soon, can I collect it, and can I change my mind?
Having the information isn’t enough. An agent needs information, context, rules, and operational capabilities to resolve a customer’s decision. For now, most stores that look ready by default are only ready until the buyer asks a real question.
One thing our test did not measure, and that surprised me most in hindsight: we told each store exactly which item to buy. A real buyer rarely arrives with a variant ID. They need help choosing between sizes, models, and related products, and that decision logic is merchant knowledge no platform can install by default. Shopify can carry it; only the merchant can write it. That’s the next test, and the subject of a future column.
Methodology: 122 leading Shopify storefronts, selected from published rankings of top Shopify merchants, probed between August and September 2026. The layers tested were: agents.md, llms.txt, UCP profiles and MCP tool listings; product-page structured data; the visible text of policy pages; the buyer questions and control questions put to each store’s own policy tool; a non-completing checkout lifecycle test (never calling complete_checkout or sending payment); a static-HTML accessibility check of each product page; and, on September 30, a browser check of the new WebMCP checkout tools at two stores, reading the checkout without submitting it. Requests were rate-limited, and responses that were throttled or blocked were recorded as unknown rather than absent. Coverage varies by test: policy text for 56 stores, policy tool for 88, live checkout for 74, product-page accessibility for 68. Shipping was tested to one Boston address. The accessibility check reads server HTML only, so it understates what JavaScript may add.

title: Building trust through social media: 5 ways to earn it
content:
Authenticity is the most important brand characteristic on social media, according to Sprout’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey . But as audiences grow more skeptical of what they see in their feeds, brands need to work harder to earn their trust.
People rely on social media for news, product recommendations and connection. At the same time, Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 35% of users trust social media less than they did a year ago. AI-generated content adds to that skepticism, making it harder to distinguish real experiences from manufactured ones.
Sprout’s Be So FR webinar explored this “trust recession” and the growing demand for content that reflects real people and experiences. Brands need to show who’s behind their content and follow through when customers reach out.
Building trust through social media starts with what you publish and how you respond to your audience. In this guide, we’ll explore what earns audience trust and practical ways to strengthen it.
People often encounter your brand through someone else’s post before they visit your website. They search for recommendations, compare customer experiences and ask questions in the comments. Those interactions help them decide whether to trust you.
Sprout’s 2026 Pulse Surveys show how people use social to find information and decide what to buy:
These social media statistics show why brands need to pay attention to conversations beyond their own accounts. With influencers playing such a significant role in what people buy, choosing credible partners matters.
For example, viewers of @theglownarrative’s skincare review discuss product prices, share what they want to try and recommend alternatives. Her review gives viewers a starting point, while the comments offer additional perspectives. Brands that partner with creators who share honest, firsthand experiences give potential customers more reason to trust their products.
The same online scrutiny applies when something goes wrong for a brand too. According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, consumers first hear about a brand crisis on social. And 64% say it’s important for brands to respond publicly on social rather than through a press release or website statement.
Social media’s influence gives brands a chance to turn audience trust into growth. When people trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products and recommend them to others. As Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey highlights, creating multiple points of connection with your brand and through partnerships with trusted voices can strengthen customer relationships and support growth:
Building audience confidence starts with how your brand shows up day to day. The table below outlines four trust builders—consistency, responsiveness, transparency and proof—and the behaviors that undermine them.
A consistent voice and posting cadence set expectations for your brand. Your values need the same follow-through: if you promote a commitment to customer care, your replies should reflect it. Maintain that reliability across everyday posts, campaigns and difficult conversations.
Helpful replies show customers that you take their concerns seriously. Sprout’s Q3 pulse survey found that 38% expect a customer care response within two hours, including 14% who expect one within minutes.
For example, SpotifyCares responds to a creator’s upload problem within minutes, connects them with the right team and invites them to follow up if they run into issues.
Speed matters during crises, too, as Q2 pulse survey findings show. Acknowledge the issue promptly, explain what you know and tell people when to expect an update. The quality of your response matters as much as how quickly you send it.
Be up front about how you create your content and what you’re promoting. That includes paid partnerships, relevant AI use and the limits of your product claims.
Sprout’s Q1 pulse survey found that 28% of consumers most want brands to stop posting AI-generated content without labels. Disclose when content is AI-generated and have a person check it for accuracy before publishing. Disclosure explains how you created it, while human review reduces the risk of publishing inaccurate information.
Customer reviews and recommendations show whether your brand delivers on its promises. Sprout’s Q2 pulse survey found that 57% trust everyday users most for product recommendations, ahead of experts, mega-influencers and brand employees.
Each perspective offers something useful. Customers describe their experiences, employees explain how products work, and creators demonstrate them in use. Specific details make it easier to judge whether your product fits their needs.
Put these trust builders into practice with five steps to create credible content, choose partners and strengthen relationships with your audience.
Start with a voice your team feels comfortable using in everyday conversations. Sprout’s Q3 pulse survey found that 26% of consumers want brands to sound less corporate and 24% want them to be less salesy. Replace stock promotional language with specific, useful information about your products and the people who use them.
Assess recent posts for language that feels forced or interchangeable with another brand. Give your team examples of how your voice translates into captions and customer replies. Before joining a trend, ask whether it fits your brand and gives your audience something worthwhile.
Read comments and customer care messages for recurring questions. To get a fuller picture of what people want, look beyond those who contact you directly. Social listening expands that research by tracking conversations about your brand, industry and competitors. It reveals common concerns and unmet audience needs.
With Sprout Social Listening , your team can explore those conversations by topic, compare themes and track sentiment over time. Use it to investigate recurring frustrations or questions that your content hasn’t addressed.
Use those findings to make a concrete change. Repeated setup questions might call for a tutorial. Pricing confusion might reveal information missing from your website. Share relevant feedback with the teams responsible for resolving it.
Close the loop by explaining how audience feedback influenced your decision.
Look for creators whose content and expertise fit your brand. Sprout’s 2026 Influencer Marketing Report found that 47% of consumers consider a creator’s topics when deciding whether to follow them, compared with only 17% who consider follower count. Prioritize relevant expertise and audience fit when building your shortlist.
Examine potential partners’ recent posts, past sponsorships and responses to criticism. Check whether they make accurate claims and disclose paid relationships. These details help you assess their credibility and identify potential brand safety concerns.
Sprout Social Influencer Marketing automates creator evaluation and partnership management. Customizable Brand Safety Reports flag content that needs a closer look, while Creator Hub supports content submissions and approvals.
Once you’ve chosen a creator, give them time to get familiar with your product so they have something meaningful to share. Agree on disclosure requirements and accurate claims, then leave room for their perspective. A demonstration or thoughtful review will be more useful to their audience when it reflects their experience.
Invite customers to share how they use your products, then ask permission to feature their posts and credit their work. Choose examples that show the product’s value, such as a customer explaining how it solves a particular problem.
Employees also bring firsthand knowledge to your content. Sprout’s 2026 Influencer Marketing Report found that 46% of consumers most want to hear from frontline employees. Invite employees to demonstrate products or answer questions customers regularly ask.
Make participation voluntary and provide time and support to contribute. Also consider additional compensation: 61% of consumers believe employees should receive extra pay for promoting their company on social.
Give people ways to connect around interests they share with your brand. Invite them to exchange advice, share their work or help develop an idea. Respond to their contributions and recognize useful discussions.
Notion’s Earth Day Instagram post offers an example: it features community-built templates and directs followers to those resources. Members contribute tools other users can put to work, and Notion gives those contributions visibility.
Start with a recurring activity your team can support, such as a monthly member showcase or an expert Q&A. Keep participating between posts, so people have a reason to return and connect.
When you review your social strategy, consider whether each interaction gives people more confidence in your brand. Did your content help someone make a decision? Did your response resolve their concern? Have you delivered what you promised?
These questions keep trust connected to the customer’s experience. Use them to identify what deserves more investment and where your approach needs to change.
For more insight into the voices consumers trust and what they expect from brand partnerships, explore Sprout’s 2026 Influencer Marketing Report .
Brand trust on social media is the confidence people have that your brand shares accurate information and follows through on its commitments. It develops through the content you publish, how you respond to customers and what others say about their experiences with your business.
People use social media to research products and compare experiences before buying. Trust gives them confidence to consider your brand, act on recommendations and return after a positive experience.
Track sentiment, recurring themes in customer feedback and the quality of conversations about your brand. Combine social listening findings with customer surveys that ask directly about trust. Monitor changes over time, especially after campaigns or service improvements, rather than treating engagement alone as proof of trust.
How do you rebuild brand trust on social media after a crisis?
Acknowledge the issue promptly, take responsibility for your brand’s role and explain what you’re doing to address it. Answer questions with verified information and provide updates as you make progress. Follow through on promised changes and show evidence that you’ve resolved the problem.
